articles.summary: ITANAGAR: Sikkim-based rapper Ugen Namgyal Bhutia, popularly known as UNB, was allegedly attacked by a group of men in Arunachal Pradesh’s Lower Diban.
articles.body: ITANAGAR: Sikkim-based rapper Ugen Namgyal Bhutia, popularly known as UNB, was allegedly attacked by a group of men in Arunachal Pradesh’s Lower Dibang Valley district, police said on Wednesday.The incident occurred around 6pm on Monday near Tiwari Gaon when UNB and his team were returning to Roing after attending a festival in Anini, police said.Two vehicles allegedly followed their car for nearly an hour before intercepting it on an isolated stretch.Eight to 10 men allegedly vandalised UNB’s vehicle with a rod and attacked him and his manager, police said.UNB suffered injuries to his head and face, besides swelling around one eye, police said.The attackers fled after spotting a truck approaching the area, they added.The incident was reported to Roing police station around 7.50pm.Police attributed the delay in reporting the incident to poor mobile connectivity in the area.Following the complaint, police alerted check gates and asked personnel to look out for vehicles matching the description provided by the victims.UNB’s manager alleged that the attackers had covered their vehicles’ number plates with mud and intercepted their car after confirming that the rapper was travelling in it.Roing police station officer-in-charge Taniya Uli said police accompanied UNB and his team to the site on Tuesday as part of the investigation.The isolated location, absence of eyewitnesses and poor network connectivity were posing challenges to the investigation, the officer said.A case has been registered under provisions relating to wrongful restraint, voluntarily causing hurt and criminal intimidation, he said.Police said they were working to ascertain the motive behind the attack and establish the identity of the accused.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Itanagar news. articles.title: US-Iran talks: What was discussed in Trump's 'good meeting' on the sidelines of UNGA
articles.summary: Middle East News: US President Donald Trump said US and Iranian officials held an unexpected meeting on Tuesday, even as he warned in his address to the UN General Asse.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump said US and Iranian officials held an unexpected meeting on Tuesday, even as he warned in his address to the UN General Assembly that he could “annihilate” Iran if a deal is not reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.Trump said his chief envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, held talks with Iranian officials for about three hours on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders.Trump described the meeting as positive, saying, “It was a very good meeting.” He later added that the Iranian officials were “not the highest level, but it’s something.”What happened in the meetingUS Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff said in a post on X that the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the US and Iranian teams. He said he felt “very good” about the meeting and was hopeful the effort “will prove constructive and promising.”Iranian officials confirmed that foreign minister Abbas Araghchi took part in the talks, which were mediated by Qatari diplomats.Iran conveyed several conditions during the talks, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to what Tehran described as US “acts of aggression,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told state news agency IRNA.Baghaei said Tehran also called for an end to the naval blockade and economic warfare, along with the release of Iranian assets, IRNA reported.A senior Iranian official separately said Tehran was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington took reciprocal steps to ease military and economic pressure on Iran, as cited by the Guardian.The official said the position had been approved by Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and the Supreme National Security Council.Earlier, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said there was no contradiction between pursuing negotiations and continuing the war. The position was also echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Ghalibaf in recent remarks to the Iranian parliament.The Iranian official said Tehran was looking for signs that Washington was prepared to resume negotiations, lift its military blockade of Iranian ports and halt operations linked to the Strait of Hormuz. If the US took those steps, Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, the official said.However, some Iranian media outlets close to the IRGC denied that any new position had been adopted, highlighting differences within Tehran.Trump warns Iran of 'annihilation'In his address to the General Assembly, Trump defended his decision to launch the war with Iran, saying he had shown resolve while other leaders had hesitated.At the same time, he suggested the conflict could be approaching a turning point, calling on Iran to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to negotiations to reach a settlement.“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”“The terrorist regime is behaving badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate," Trump added.Most members of Iran’s delegation walked out of the chamber as Trump criticised the Islamic Republic in his address.War continues to pressure energy marketsThe conflict has grown more complicated despite US and Israeli strikes that have killed much of Iran’s top leadership and damaged its air force and navy, while a US blockade on Iranian oil has further strained Tehran’s economy.The war has also kept energy markets on edge, with oil prices remaining elevated. Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia shut a key pipeline that had served as an alternative route for oil stranded in the Gulf after it came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.Meanwhile, territorial advances by Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iran-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait have made the Red Sea shipping route increasingly hazardous for oil carriers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2025, an Oxfam shop found a rare Chinese Bible in a donation pile; estimated at £800, it sold for £56,280
articles.summary: UK News: A rare 2-volume Bible donated to an Oxfam bookshop in Chelmsford, Essex, sold for £56,280 at auction after volunteers spotted it in a pile of donation.
articles.body: A rare 2-volume Bible donated to an Oxfam bookshop in Chelmsford, Essex, sold for £56,280 at auction after volunteers spotted it in a pile of donations. Dating from 1815 to 1822, the Bible contains a Chinese translation produced by missionaries John Lassar and Joshua Marshman and was printed in Serampore, India. It had been estimated at £600 to £800 by Bonhams before the auction, but attracted two weeks of online bidding before selling for £56,280 on March 20, 2025. Oxfam said the proceeds from the sale would support its work tackling poverty and inequality.Volunteers spotted the Bible before it reached the shelvesThe Bible was discovered by Oxfam volunteers Chris Tyrrell and Eleanor Atack at the charity's Chelmsford bookshop. They suspected that the unusual volumes could be valuable and kept them from being placed on the shop floor for an ordinary sale. The discovery was subsequently referred for specialist assessment, with Bonhams putting an estimate of £600 to £800 on the Bible before the auction. The final price was more than 70 times the top end of that estimate. The online auction ran for two weeks before closing on March 20, 2025, when the Bible sold for £56,280. Oxfam's Chelmsford shop manager Nick Reeves said the team had been surprised by how high the bidding climbed.The Bible dates back to the early 19th centuryThe 2-volume work dates from 1815 to 1822 and was translated by John Lassar and Joshua Marshman. The translation was produced in Serampore, India, where Marshman was part of the Baptist missionary community that established the Serampore mission and later founded Serampore College. The Bible was published in a series of parts, with the Pentateuch appearing first in 1817. Bonhams described the completed work as the first complete Bible in Chinese. Lassar, an Armenian scholar, collaborated with Marshman on the Chinese translation. The work was produced at a time when Serampore had become an important centre for missionary printing and translation in the region.The rare book vastly exceeded its auction estimateBefore the sale, Bonhams estimated the Bible at between £600 and £800. The eventual £56,280 price represented a dramatic increase over that valuation. The Bible was sold as part of a Bonhams auction featuring rare books donated to Oxfam shops. Oxfam said the Bible was among 23 other books, meaning 24 Oxfam books were represented in the sale altogether. Together, the books raised more than £105,000 for the charity. Other notable works offered in the auction included books by Charles Dickens, Jane Austen, J.R.R. Tolkien and Roald Dahl. The collection included a first edition of A Christmas Carol, a first edition of Pride and Prejudice, a first edition of The Lord of the Rings and a signed copy of Matilda.Oxfam's rare-book sales turn donations into fundsThe Chinese Bible was an unusually valuable discovery, but Oxfam regularly sends particularly rare or collectable donated books to specialist auction houses rather than selling them through its ordinary shops. Ian Falkingham, Oxfam's donated goods strategy lead specialising in books, said the charity was grateful for the rare and unusual books donated to its shops. For the Chelmsford team, the Bible demonstrated the potential value hidden among ordinary donations. What initially appeared to be an old pair of books in a pile of donated material ultimately became the most valuable item in the auction, generating £56,280 for Oxfam's charitable work.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Divorced woman can seek maintenance even if divorce was on ground of desertion: Allahabad HC
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: The Allahabad High Court’s Lucknow Bench has held that a divorced woman can demand maintenance from her former husband even if the divorce wa.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: The Allahabad High Court’s Lucknow Bench has held that a divorced woman can demand maintenance from her former husband even if the divorce was granted to the husband on the ground of desertion, if she has not remarried and is unable to maintain herself.Justice Ram Manohar Narayan Mishra made the observation while allowing a criminal revision petition filed by Suneeta against an order of the Family Court, Sultanpur, which had rejected her maintenance claim.The woman had filed a maintenance case under Section 125 CrPC in 2009, alleging that her husband and in-laws had harassed her over additional dowry and demanded Rs 1 lakh, a motorcycle and a colour television. The husband denied the allegations and claimed that she had deserted him and was unwilling to live with him.During the proceedings, the husband obtained an ex-parte divorce decree on September 25, 2014, on the ground of desertion. The bench also noted material indicating that he had subsequently remarried and that the name of the second woman had been recorded as his wife in his service records.Delivering the verdict, the bench held that a divorced woman continues to be treated as a wife for the limited purpose of claiming maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. The mere fact that the divorce was granted on the ground of desertion does not, by itself, bar her claim.The court observed that a divorced woman is entitled to maintenance until she remarries or becomes capable of maintaining herself through her own earnings, subject to the applicable legal conditions.It held that the Family Court had erred in rejecting the woman's claim in toto. While the court said her entitlement for the period before the divorce would have to be examined separately, it directed that her claim from September 25, 2014, the date of divorce, be considered afresh.The court also held that her minor son was entitled to maintenance until attaining majority, after accounting for any amount already received through Army authorities.The matter was remanded to the Family Court for fresh consideration. Meanwhile, pending fresh adjudication by the family Court , the bench has directed the husband to pay Rs 4,000 per month as interim maintenance to the woman.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: 'White House access privilege, not right': DOJ cites national security behind Trump barring reporters
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration has told a federal court that the president can restrict reporters’ access to the White House, including on the basis of thei.
articles.body: The Trump administration has told a federal court that the president can restrict reporters’ access to the White House, including on the basis of their reporting, arguing that protecting national security gives him broad authority over who can enter the complex.In a court filing late Tuesday, the Justice Department argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right” and said the administration could deny journalists access to restricted presidential areas even for “viewpoint-discriminatory reasons”.The filing came hours before an emergency hearing in Washington over the Trump administration’s decision to revoke the White House hard passes of CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The three news organisations are asking the court to restore their access.The administration has argued that the journalists’ reporting on sensitive and classified information has raised national security concerns.Also read: ‘You shouldn’t be here covering me’ - Trump confronts CNN’s Kaitlan Collins at UN amid White House banWhat the DOJ is arguingThe Justice Department said the White House is a highly controlled government facility and argued that First Amendment protections do not give journalists an independent right to access it.Citing previous court rulings, the DOJ said the First Amendment does not create a right for journalists to enter the White House or obtain government information simply because they are members of the press.The filing also argued that the White House can impose standards on journalists receiving hard passes and that the president can determine whether reporters meet those standards.According to the filing, the administration considers the publication of classified or sensitive national security information a violation of the standards expected of journalists granted access to the White House.The DOJ said the government had two “compelling reasons” for restricting the journalists’ access: enforcing minimum standards of professionalism and protecting classified information.The administration also argued that the president has constitutional authority to protect information relating to national security. The filing cited a Supreme Court ruling recognising the president’s authority to classify and control access to national-security information.The DOJ further said the president had determined that reporting by the three organisations had threatened national security, including reports involving sensitive information about the White House complex.Also read: ‘Dangerous for our Country’ - Trump slams CNN, Politico, MS NOW over White House lawsuitWhy did Trump revoke the hard passes?The White House press office said in letters to CNN, MS NOW and Politico that the president had decided to revoke their hard passes because they had allegedly violated standards of professionalism and decorum.The letters accused the organisations of publishing sensitive or classified information and, in some cases, spreading what the administration described as false information about national security.For CNN, the White House cited reports including a January story about construction details of a “top-secret” bunker beneath the White House east wing and an August report that US missile-defence interceptor stocks had been significantly depleted.The letter to Politico cited, among other reports, coverage of White House plans involving Secret Service security improvements and reports about US military weapons stocks.The MS NOW letter similarly cited reports involving alleged FBI leak investigations and US military munitions.The White House has given the three organisations until Friday to contest the decision and the factual basis cited in the letters.Also read: 'Will protect our 1st amendment right' - CNN, MS NOW & Politico to sue Trump admin over White House banPress groups seek immediate restoration of accessCNN, MS NOW and Politico have challenged the restrictions in federal court, arguing that the administration is retaliating against them because of their reporting.The dispute has already affected White House coverage, with major television networks, National Public Radio and White House photographers suspending or reducing live coverage in response to the restrictions, according to CNN.The federal court in Washington has previously intervened when administrations sought to restrict journalists’ White House access. The current case is therefore shaping up as a major test of how far presidential control over the White House extends when it comes into conflict with press freedom and due process protections.The emergency hearing before US district judge Timothy Kelly is expected to determine whether the three organisations will regain access while the broader legal fight continues.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Major banks around the world including NatWest, Bank of America, ING, Capital One, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, and New Zealand’s ASB Bank have issued a joint warning that AI-powered shopping bots could expose consumers to scams, fraud, and data-privacy breaches, as reported by Reuters. The warning from the banks comes as tech giants like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta are increasingly promoting AI agents as shopping tools, whereas retailers race to influence chatbot recommendations. As per the Reuters report, British retailer John Lewis reported that searches originating from AI agents jumped to 2.5% this year, up from just 0.3% a year ago. "They are concerned that AI agents may buy the wrong thing or spend too much – or even worse, lose their money to scams and fraud. They are not sure whether they will be protected or who they will need to go to if things ⁠go wrong," said Bank of America. What the banks are worried aboutIn a new report, the banking coalition acknowledged that customers are genuinely enthusiastic about the potential of AI-driven shopping and eager to adopt it. But the report was equally clear that adoption is outpacing both industry standards and consumer protections, leaving a meaningful trust gap between what AI agents promise and what safeguards currently exist.The report noted that consumers remain unsure whether AI will actually act in their best interests, worrying that AI agents could buy the wrong item, overspend, or — in the worst case — lose their money to scams and fraud altogether, with little clarity on whether they'd be protected or who to turn to if something goes wrong.Specific risks flagged in the report include AI agents requesting and directly entering customers' card details into websites without adequate oversight, as well as agents potentially steering shoppers toward payment methods that offer weaker fraud protections than more secure alternatives.What the banks want to see happenThe coalition plans to bring a set of proposals to policymakers, including mandatory disclosure whenever an AI agent is involved in a transaction, greater transparency into how these agents actually make purchasing decisions, and stronger safeguards around customer data protection.The report also argued that both consumers and merchants should retain the freedom to choose which AI-powered e-commerce services they use, and called for different AI shopping systems to be interoperable with one another — rather than locking users into a single ecosystem's tools.Proposed safeguardsTo mitigate risks, banks plan to discuss proposals with policymakers, including:* Mandatory disclosure when an AI agent is involved in a transaction.* Greater transparency on how AI agents make decisions.* Stronger safeguards to protect customer data.* Ensuring consumers and merchants can freely choose which AI-powered services to use.* Interoperability across different AI commerce systems.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Tasmanian devils lived in Australia’s Pilbara for at least 45,000 years before disappearing from mainland Australia 3,200 years ago
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Archaeologists found the first clear evidence that Tasmanian devils once lived in the Pilbara region of northwestern Australia. The evidence comes fro.
articles.body: Archaeologists found the first clear evidence that Tasmanian devils once lived in the Pilbara region of northwestern Australia. The evidence comes from Juukan Gorge on Puutu Kunti Kurrama Country, where excavations recovered two diagnostic devil specimens from different periods. One is a right dentary fragment with the first and second lower molars from Holocene sediments.The other is an incomplete lower premolar from Late Pleistocene sediments. According to research published by the University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney) in Archaeology in Oceania titled ‘First Record of Tasmanian Devils in the Pilbara: Late Quaternary Subfossils From Juukan Gorge, Puutu Kunti Kurrama Country, and Insights Into Human-Faunal Relationships and Extinction’, show that Tasmanian devils occupied arid inland Australia.What do the fossil teeth reveal about Tasmanian devils at Juukan GorgeThe study identifies the Juukan Gorge remains as Tasmanian devils based on diagnostic dental features. The dentary fragment preserves the first and second lower molars. Its robust molars, reduced metaconids, slight posterior cingulids, well-developed dental structures, and buccally positioned hypoconids distinguish it from thylacines and quolls. The second specimen is a fragment of a lower first or second premolar. Its robust, low-crowned form resembles that of Sarcophilus, while the tooth crown is positioned buccally, away from the long axis of the dentary. A small enamel protuberance also resembles the buccal cingulid found in Sarcophilus. The researchers note that the premolar identification is tentative because enamel flaking obscures its complete condition and creates a size discrepancy.What do the two Juukan Gorge specimens reveal about their ageThe two specimens come from different layers at the Juukan 2 rock shelter. The dentary was recovered from Holocene sediments and is associated with charcoal. The premolar came from Late Pleistocene sediments and was dated using optically stimulated luminescence. Reportedly, two samples placed the specimen’s age at more than 42,000 and 47,000 years ago.The researchers say the oldest specimen provides evidence of Tasmanian devils in the Pilbara before the Last Glacial Maximum, while the younger dentary confirms their presence during the Holocene. Direct dating of the specimens was not considered appropriate because of cultural sensitivities surrounding destructive sampling methods. The researchers found minimal signs of bioturbation or major post-depositional disturbance nearby.Chewed and digested bones show long interaction between devils and humansThe researchers examined bones showing marks linked to devil activity. Chewed bones were assessed for tooth-mark pits and scores, while digested bones were identified through surface pitting or polish. The study reports numerous devil-derived traces throughout the archaeological sequence, including chewed and digested bone fragments. These traces indicate sustained interaction between humans and devils over at least 45,000 years.The consistent occurrence of bones modified by devil scavenging of human butchery waste indicates that the animals relied, at least partly, on resources produced by people from the time humans arrived in the Pilbara. The findings point to an ecological association between the two groups at Juukan Gorge.Factors that led to the extinction of Tasmanian devilsThe findings also address the disappearance of Tasmanian devils from mainland Australia. The study places their mainland extinction at about 3,200 years ago, with the best estimate at 3,179-3,227 years ago. The researchers note that the cause of the mainland extinction remains under debate. One prevailing hypothesis links the disappearance of devils and thylacines to the arrival of dingoes about 4,000 years ago, either through direct predation or competition for niche space. Other proposed explanations include changes in human hunting technology, increased resource use, and climate instability, as well as combinations of these factors.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Strategic desperation': Iran on Trump's 'annihilate Islamic Republic' remark
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran has hit back at US President Donald Trump's threat to \"annihilate\" the Islamic Republic, accusing Washington of showing strategic desperation rat.
articles.body: Iran has hit back at US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic, accusing Washington of showing strategic desperation rather than strength as tensions between the two countries remain high.In a statement issued after Trump's address to the United Nations General Assembly, Iran's Armed Forces said the US president's repeated threats were aimed more at domestic political messaging than reflecting the situation on the ground.The statement was issued by the General Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces and the Khatam al-Anbya Central Headquarters, according to Iran's state-run IRNA news agency.Iran calls Trump's threat 'strategic desperation'Iranian military authorities said Trump's remarks showed the difficulties facing the US in its confrontation with Iran. They argued that repeated threats were not evidence of American strength, but reflected what they described as exhaustion within the US military.The statement also accused the US of creating instability in West Asia through its military presence in the region.Iran, it said, had instead acted as a stabilising force for regional security and international trade. It accused Washington of trying to compensate for what it described as repeated failures against Iran and the Resistance Front.The Iranian military further said Trump's words would not change the balance of power or reverse what it described as US setbacks in the conflict.Pezeshkian takes Iran's message to UNIranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrived in New York on Tuesday for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.Before leaving for the US, Pezeshkian said Iran would use international forums to present its position on the conflict and its dealings with Western powers.“We will forcefully raise Iran's positions in international forums. The issues we will raise at the United Nations are expressing the oppressed state of the Iranian nation, the crimes that have occurred, and the distrust that has been created. We went to the negotiating table several times and signed agreements, but unfortunately, the whole world saw how commitments were not fulfilled and the writings were trampled underfoot," he said en-route to the US.The Iranian Armed Forces said Pezeshkian's UN address would also convey what it described as the strength and resilience of the Iranian people.Trump presents Iran with choiceTrump had used his UNGA speech to issue a direct warning to Tehran, saying Iran faced a choice between reaching a deal and facing further US military action.“I have a big decision to make. Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? But I believe we'll make a deal right after the election, because it doesn't make sense for them not to,” Trump said.The exchange comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran, with both sides using increasingly forceful language as diplomatic efforts over the conflict remain under pressure.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Operation Sindoor lessons baked in to IAF's multilateral Tarang Shakti wargames
articles.summary: News News: India will put the operational lessons of Operation Sindoor to test on a much bigger stage when the multi-nation air exercise Tarang Shakti kicks off .
articles.body: India will put the operational lessons of Operation Sindoor to test on a much bigger stage when the multi-nation air exercise Tarang Shakti kicks off at the Indian Air Force base in Jodhpur from September 26 to October 11. Around 40 countries, including the US, France and Germany, are expected to take part, making it one of the largest such drills hosted by the IAF since its strikes on Pakistani airbases last May.Addressing a press conference on the scope of the exercise, IAF Vice Chief Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said Operation Sindoor had given the force valuable takeaways, even as partner nations bring their own combat experience to the table. Bringing these together in a realistic training environment, he said, would help test assumptions, challenge existing procedures and improve interoperability among participating air forces. He added that the tactics that evolved during Operation Sindoor would get reflected in the exercise, though how much each participant absorbs would depend on them.Asked whether drone warfare scenarios would be simulated, the Vice Chief indicated that all possible scenarios should be part of the drill, with broad guidelines being issued to participants. IAF officials briefing on the exercise said the drills would cover large force engagements involving high value aerial assets, air mobility operations, dynamic targeting and combat search and rescue missions, offering participants exposure across multiple facets of air operations.On the hardware front, the IAF is expected to field its Rafale and Sukhoi-30MKI fleets, while the American F-35 will make its debut on Indian soil in a military exercise, having previously only been showcased at aero-shows in Bengaluru. The IAF has already flown alongside the F-35 during exercise Pitch Black in Australia in July. Apart from the US and France, Germany, the UAE, Bangladesh, Australia and Sri Lanka will send their air assets, while 32 more countries will participate as observers.The exercise comes against the backdrop of a detailed assessment of Operation Sindoor, which flagged rapid adaptation, offensive action and stronger multi-domain capabilities as key lessons for future short, high-intensity conflicts. The operation underlined the value of surprise, concentration of force and unity of command, with the IAF quickly correcting course in the initial phase before targeting Pakistan's air defence and missile systems ahead of strikes on multiple airfields. The centralised command, distributed control and decentralised execution model was cited as a major strength, as per a report by the New Delhi based think tank the Observer Research Foundation.The importance of layered air defence system equipped with platforms such as the S-400 and Akash, managed by integrated command-and-control apparatus, proved critical against foiled Pakistani aerial offensive. The IAF is working towards integrating remotely piloted aircraft into offensive operations, expand its stock of stand-off weapons, strengthen ground-based air defence and address its shrinking fighter fleet, the same report stated.

articles.title: ‘MBS will not forget’: Ex-US official says Trump’s Houthi stance has irked Saudis
articles.summary: Middle East News: United States President Donald Trump’s decision to hold back from joining Saudi Arabia’s military campaign against the Iran-backed Houthis has created.
articles.body: United States President Donald Trump’s decision to hold back from joining Saudi Arabia’s military campaign against the Iran-backed Houthis has created a fresh strain between Washington and Riyadh, adding another complication to an already uneasy relationship.Saudi Arabia has asked the US to carry out repeated air strikes against the Houthis, according to a person familiar with the discussions. Washington has so far declined, leaving Riyadh to confront an expanding threat largely on its own.The hesitation is particularly significant for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has spent years relying on the US as Saudi Arabia’s main security partner while also trying to position the kingdom as a major global centre for business, trade and tourism.Saudi Arabia wants stronger US backingThe Houthis have intensified attacks on Saudi targets after declaring a blockade of the kingdom’s ports in July. Over the past two weeks, they have struck oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia and launched an offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.The offensive has pushed back Saudi-backed forces supporting Yemen’s government and strengthened Houthi control around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's key shipping routes.The Houthis also fired a ballistic missile towards Riyadh over the weekend, marking the first such attack on the Saudi capital since the conflict resumed.Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, said the US decision was creating further uncertainty in the relationship.“The US is wavering, and ultimately its decision, at least for now, not to join the Saudis is simply injecting more tension into the bilateral relationship,” she told FT. “It’s raising further concerns for the Saudis about what role they can rely on the US to play.”Retired Lieutenant General Karen Gibson, a former director of intelligence at US Central Command, said the episode could leave a lasting impression on the Saudi leadership.“MBS will not forget this,” Gibson said, adding that the hesitation shows that the “United States will not necessarily fight when Saudi Arabia believes its vital interests are threatened”.Trump faces pressure on another frontTrump's reluctance to intervene directly comes as his administration is already dealing with the wider conflict with Iran.Saudi Arabia has itself faced repeated Iranian strikes on infrastructure, while the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has added to the economic pressure affecting the Gulf.Trump also abandoned a US military plan in May to escort commercial shipping through the strait after Riyadh refused to allow American aircraft to use Saudi bases or airspace for the operation. Saudi officials had expressed concerns that the plan could trigger further attacks on Gulf states.Washington is also dealing with limited military resources and depleted ammunition stocks. Liz Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said opening another front would be politically difficult with US midterm elections approaching in November.“It would be really difficult for [Trump] to get involved in yet another front of this war” ahead of the US midterm elections in November.However, she said the possibility remained that the Saudi request could be narrowed enough for Trump to accept.“It’s very possible that [MBS] is slowly reducing the ask and that Trump will at some point see something that is politically feasible for him,” Dent said.“There’s a lot more going on behind the scenes that’s keeping that relationship intact,” she added.Defence ties remain intactDespite the disagreement, Washington has not abandoned Riyadh. The US continues to supply Saudi Arabia with weapons and intelligence, while Saudi forces also rely on American air-defence systems.The Trump administration last week approved a potential $24.3bn sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, although the aircraft would take years to be delivered.A Saudi analyst, who declined to be named, said Riyadh remained frustrated but understood Trump's approach.“There is a certain amount of frustration, but there’s also a recognition that’s the way [Trump] is,” the analyst told FT. “Saudi Arabia has all the capacity to bomb everything, and the US is giving us targeting information we need.”The analyst said American aircraft could nevertheless have played an important symbolic role at the beginning of the conflict.The US has also maintained contact with the Houthis through talks facilitated by Oman. A Houthi official told the Associated Press that the group was targeting Saudi vessels and would not attack US or other international ships. Trump has also said the Houthis agreed not to target American interests.But analysts said the limits of US involvement could have longer-term consequences.Yacoubian said it “does not instil a lot of confidence in the partnership” if Saudi Arabia “is going to be left out on their own because US assets are not currently threatened by this Houthi onslaught”.Asaad al-Shamlan of the Prince Saud al-Faisal Institute for Diplomatic Studies said the broader relationship remained “in a very good state”. But he noted that Riyadh viewed the Houthi threat differently from Washington and Europe, where it is often seen mainly as a Saudi problem.Firas Maksad, managing director for Middle East and North Africa at Eurasia Group, said the disagreement could push Saudi Arabia further towards diversifying its security partnerships.“The space it leaves behind will create opportunities for strategic competitors,” he said. “Riyadh has been diversifying its security partners while attempting an uneasy accommodation with Tehran. The tension in its relationship with Washington could accelerate that process.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Meet Caymus Maxson, the 16-year-old California teen who started Trash Turtles at 10, led 50+ beach cleanups, removed 6+ tons of debris, recycled 75,000+ cigarette butts and became a 2026 Barron Prize winner
articles.summary: US News: At 10, Caymus 'CO' Maxson noticed something wrong on a beach in Madeira Beach, Florida. In February 2020, she saw beach trash being raked towards the .
articles.body: At 10, Caymus 'CO' Maxson noticed something wrong on a beach in Madeira Beach, Florida. In February 2020, she saw beach trash being raked towards the water’s edge. She realised that the incoming tide could carry the waste into the sea and decided to act.Maxson soon started Trash Turtles, a youth-focused environmental nonprofit with the mission to 'Save the planet one piece of trash at a time'. Over the next six years, the organisation grew from a small effort on one beach into a network involved in beach cleanups, youth leadership and environmental campaigns.According to Surfrider Foundation, Trash Turtles has now hosted more than 50 beach cleanups and removed more than six tons of trash and marine debris. It has also cleaned more than 300 miles of beaches and collected more than 75,000 cigarette butts, which were recycled through TerraCycle. The organisation has also raised $8,000 to fund three water refill stations at local schools.Maxson’s work has now received national recognition. She was named among the 2026 winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which recognises young people aged 8 to 18 for making a positive impact on people and the planet. The 2026 winners include young people working in areas such as environmental protection, technology, education and community service.Small action becomes youth movementMaxson said the decision to start Trash Turtles came from seeing rubbish being pushed towards the sea. “I saw a problem with trash being raked to the water’s edge, where I knew the incoming tide could carry it out to sea, and I wanted to do something about it. That moment became the start of Trash Turtles,” Maxson said as qouted by Surfrider Foundation.The organisation’s approach is based on the idea that environmental action does not always require a large campaign or a complicated solution. It can begin with a small action, such as picking up a piece of rubbish.This idea also became the #LeaveWith3 movement. It encourages people to pick up and properly dispose of at least three extra pieces of trash wherever they are, including at school, work or the beach.“#LeaveWith3 was my way of taking a big problem and creating a simple solution that everyone could understand and participate in. The idea is that if each person picks up just three pieces of trash wherever they go, together we can leave the environment a little better than we found it,” Maxson said.More than six tons of debris removedThe numbers behind Trash Turtles show how small actions have grown over time. The organisation says it has removed more than six tons of trash and marine debris and cleaned more than 300 miles of beaches.It has also collected and recycled more than 75,000 cigarette butts through TerraCycle. Cigarette butts are among the waste items targeted by the organisation as it works to reduce pollution around coastal areas.Trash Turtles has also raised $8,000 to fund three water refill stations at local schools. The project aims to reduce reliance on single-use plastic bottles. The organisation has awarded $8,500 through its Hope Scholarship programme to eight young people.“What started with picking up trash on one beach has become so much more than I ever imagined. It showed me that one small idea can grow into something that reaches people far beyond where it started,” Maxson said.Focus on plastic wasteBeach cleanups are only one part of Trash Turtles’ work. Its Straw Change Campaign focuses on single-use plastic waste, including discarded plastic straws and packaging associated with products such as Capri Sun.The organisation’s approach involves identifying an environmental problem, documenting it, educating people about it and asking for change. Its work therefore goes beyond simply removing waste from beaches.Trash Turtles also focuses on helping young people understand that they can participate in solving environmental problems in their own communities.Maxson has been involved with Jane Goodall’s Roots & Shoots USA and is serving her second term on the National Roots & Shoots Youth Council. She also took part in youth leadership activities, including the 2024 Hope in Action Summit at Tropicana Field.“Young people can bring a different perspective, and our voices can make a real difference,” Maxson says.Moving to CaliforniaTrash Turtles has developed partnerships and collaborations with organisations including the Jane Goodall Institute’s Roots & Shoots USA, Clearwater Marine Aquarium, Tampa Bay Watch, Keep Pinellas Beautiful, Surfing’s Evolution, Preservation Foundation and Phillps. It has also worked with sustainable brands.Maxson has also worked on environmental storytelling and media projects. Along the way, she has met and collaborated with people including Dr Jane Goodall, Ian Somerhalder and Caulin Donaldson of Trash Caulin.The organisation has now moved its headquarters from Florida to Pacific Grove, California, bringing its youth-focused approach to ocean conservation to Monterey Bay.“I have come to understand that environmental issues usually stem from a normalization of everyday systems that have never been challenged,” Maxson said. “That realization makes me hopeful, because it means that change is only one choice away,” she said.Trash Turtles joined Surfrider Monterey for California Coastal Cleanup Day on Saturday at Sand City.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran’s president to address UN as Trump mixes threats and diplomacy
articles.summary: Push to end the Iran war looms over UNGA’s second day. Meanwhile Ukraine’s Zelensky and Venezuela’s Rodriguez are also set to speak in New York. Follow for the latest updates.
articles.body:
• US-Iran diplomacy: Iran’s leadership has warned the US against any fresh attacks after President Donald Trump said in his speech to the UN General Assembly that he faced a decision between annihilating the country or making a deal. His special envoy Steve Witkoff said US and Iranian delegations held lengthy talks on the sidelines through mediators.

• Who we’re watching: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will be among the world leaders addressing UNGA today , followed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said he was ready for trilateral talks with Russia and US to end the war in Ukraine.

• Eyes on Venezuela: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez will address UNGA more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, who is currently being held in a Brooklyn detention center just miles away. Trump met with her last night as Washington maintains political pressure on her country to enact reforms.

US President Donald Trump touted his Board of Peace during his remarks to the United Nations General Assembly yesterday, calling it a “significant group of people.”

Earlier this year, Trump said that the international body he formed to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza, “might” one day replace the United Nations.

But as Trump and other world leaders on the board attend this week’s General Debate, the Board of Peace has struggled to make tangible progress on peace efforts in the Middle East, and questions linger about its mission and effectiveness.

There will be a “high-level” briefing for the Board of Peace this week, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.

What is the Board of Peace? Trump initially pitched the board as a group overseeing the reconstruction of the Gaza Strip, but its stated mission has since expanded to tackle conflicts the world over.

Members of the panel, which Trump chairs, include several Gulf states, Turkey, Pakistan, Argentina and others, but most of the US’ European allies have not joined. Permanent membership carried a $1 billion price tag .

Despite major financial and personnel commitments Trump says board members have pledged, tangible progress has been scarce. The board still has yet to enter Gaza, and Israeli attacks on the Palestinian enclave have continued.

In July, Trump said the Board of Peace had reached a breakthrough in Gaza that involved Hamas surrendering its weapons as part of a 15-point peace plan . A senior Hamas official said that commitment was contingent on Israel upholding its obligations under the October ceasefire agreement.

But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in August that Israel rejected the peace plan , demanding the full disarmament of Hamas before any Israeli forces withdraw.

CNN’s Jennifer Hansler, Kylie Atwood, Helen Regan, Kara Fox, Alejandra Jaramillo, Jeremy Diamond, Tal Shalev and Oren Liebermann contributed reporting.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is expected to speak at today’s United Nations General Assembly, nearly seven months since US-Israeli strikes started the war with Iran.

Here are some of the latest developments on the conflict:

Despite the US and Iran reaching a memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the war back in June, fighting has continued in the months since.

US President Donald Trump announced that the ceasefire was “OVER! ” in early July, after Iran’s targeting of three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz prompted an exchange of strikes .

In subsequent months, Trump stressed his disinterest in diplomacy and instructed US officials to end talks. Earlier this month, however, he said he was open to the “concept” of reopening negotiations with Iran.

Yesterday, Trump said that he has a “big decision” to make on Iran — casting it as a choice between striking a deal after the US midterm elections in November or annihilating Iran.

Later in the day, he said that members of his administration met with the Iranian delegation at the UN General Assembly for about three hours, in what he described as a “very good meeting.”

Meanwhile, Iranian officials have met with their counterparts in countries including Oman, the United Arab Emirates, and China in recent weeks.

In comments made at the start of this month, Pezeshkian said that, if the US “returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding,” his country “will immediately reciprocate.”

Since the ceasefire broke down in July, the US has launched a number of attacks on Iran, with Tehran also targeting American bases in the region and vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Then, after a period of relative calm lasting for more than a month, the US and Iran began exchanging regular strikes at the end of August.

On August 30, the US military stuck Iran’s Larak Island, where it said forces were observed preparing to launch mines into the strait.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) vowed retaliation, firing missiles into Jordan, though they were intercepted, according to a US official.

In an update on September 8, the US military said it had “destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers” after the IRGC “targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles.”

Fighting has appears to have quietened, with no US strikes on Iran being publicly reported for more than two weeks.

CNN’s Kevin Liptak, Mostafa Salem, Aida Karimi, Maureen Chowdhury and Kit Maher contributed to this reporting.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said he will use his General Assembly address to highlight the deaths of dozens of children in a strike on an elementary school in southern Iran at the outset of the war.

On February 28, at the start of the US-Iran war, the US struck the Shajareh Tayyiba school in Minab, southern Iran, while the US military was attacking a neighboring Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps facility, CNN has reported. At least 156 people, including 120 children and 26 teachers, were killed, according to Iranian officials.

The strike was considered one of the worst civilian casualty incidents in recent US military history.

In March, two sources briefed on the preliminary findings of an ongoing internal investigation told CNN that US Central Command created target coordinates for the strike that hit the school using outdated information provided by the Defense Intelligence Agency, which contributed to the mistake.

US President Donald Trump had initially asserted that Iran might be to blame for the strike, though when pressed on why no one in his own administration seemed to be publicly supporting that claim, he responded: “Because I just don’t know enough about it.”

The Pentagon’s internal investigation remains stuck in limbo , as the stage where Defense Intelligence Agency analysts review satellite imagery and other intelligence sources has not yet been ordered by the Pentagon, three sources familiar with the matter told CNN in July.

This month, a United Nations fact-finding mission concluded in a new report that the strike may have been a war crime. The findings by the UN’s Independent International Fact-Finding Mission still need to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council, but could later be used by international courts like the International Criminal Court.

The leaders of Ukraine and Iran are set to speak at the United Nations General Assembly today amid a pair of ongoing conflicts that, while separate, have contributed to tensions between the countries.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, while Iran has been at war with the US and Israel since late February this year.

Though Tehran and Kyiv are nearly 1,500 miles apart as the crow flies, the wars have overlapping factors, as Iran and Russia are close strategic and military allies.

Many of Russia’s attacks on Ukraine have been carried out using Iranian-made Shahed drones, and Tehran has sent missiles and other weaponry to aid Moscow’s war effort.

Shortly after the Iran war broke out earlier this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky offered to help other countries, including the US , fend off Iranian drones and missiles.

Around the same time, CNN reported that Russia was helping Iran with advanced drone tactics and providing intelligence about US military positioning.

Ukraine has posted drone experts in the Middle East to help allies counter Iranian attacks, according to Zelensky. Kyiv has also signed defense agreements with Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

In late July, tensions flared further when Ukraine struck ships in the Caspian Sea involved in transporting military goods from Iran to Russia.

Iran condemned the attack, which killed one person, and threatened retaliation .

The next day, the foreign ministers of each country held a phone call.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stressed that his country’s actions were aimed at defending Ukraine “from Russian aggression and never intended to target civilian vessels or people.” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said later that Syviha assured him the attack was unintentional.

CNN’s Kylie Atwood, Max Saltman, Nina Subkhanberdina, Natasha Bertrand, Jim Sciutto, Zachary Cohen, Jennifer Hansler, Nick Paton Walsh, Svitlana Vlasova, Victoria Butenko, Ivana Kottasová, Kosta Gak, Tim Lister, Karina Tsui, Billy Stockwell and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this reporting.

President Donald Trump may be open to meeting his Iranian counterpart at the United Nations. History suggests Tehran will not reciprocate – even under far more favorable circumstances.

The United Nations General Assembly has already provided a venue for indirect negotiations between Iranian and American officials, marking a small but significant step forward in the war. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the president himself would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

The UN has brought longtime adversaries face to face, from Bill Clinton and Fidel Castro in 2000 to Barack Obama and Raúl Castro in 2015. Yet since the Islamic Republic was founded in 1979, no Iranian president has publicly shaken hands with an American counterpart at the UN or elsewhere.

In 2000, aides reportedly choreographed an impromptu hallway handshake between President Bill Clinton and Iranian President Mohammad Khatami at the United Nations. Khatami allegedly retreated to a restroom to avoid the encounter after Tehran vetoed it. The episode came during a rare diplomatic thaw, when both presidents had been engaged in conciliatory gestures and exploring better relations.

Thirteen years later, with relations warming, speculation mounted in New York over another possible handshake, this time between Presidents Barack Obama and Hassan Rouhani, also on the sidelines of the UN gathering. The plan collapsed once more when the Iranians refused a purely symbolic gesture without a follow-up plan, while other reports cited complications “back home.”

The closest a US President has come to a shaking hands with an Iranian counterpart was in 2015, when Obama shook hands with Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif after the nuclear deal between Western powers and the Islamic Republic.

Trump tore up that agreement, imposed an unprecedented maximum pressure sanctions campaign on Iran, and launched the first direct US war on the Islamic Republic, killing its supreme leader.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s security is being provided by the US Secret Service during the United Nations General Assembly, according to American officials.

Other Iranian officials are protected by the State Department’s Diplomatic Security Service, the officials said.

The federal security services for Pezeshkian and other members of the Iranian delegation are backed up by members of the New York Police Department’s Intelligence Bureau, along with NYPD detectives and highway patrol escorts, officials told CNN.

As a founding member of the UN, Iran has maintained a presence at the global diplomatic event for decades, led most recently by the country’s president, Pezeshkian, and his predecessor, Ebrahim Raisi.

But the presence of Iran’s delegation this year , on the home turf of a country with which it remains at war , is unprecedented in recent years.

CNN’s Billy Stockwell and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.

With nearly 200 foreign dignitaries expected to be in New York City this week, security across the metropolis has been ramped up, with thousands of New York City Police Department (NYPD) officers being posted at or around UN headquarters, according to New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch.

Tisch held a security briefing on this week’s United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Thursday, where officials outlined their plans to ensure the event’s safety.

Mamdani called it an “honor” for his city to be the host of UNGA, but noted that “New York City is always a target, and especially so when thousands of international representatives are present.”

The NYPD will work alongside the US Secret Service and the State Department’s Diplomatic Security Service to protect foreign dignitaries during the assembly, he said.

Mamdani stressed that there are “no known specific or credible threats” against either UNGA or New York City, but said that “our security posture will be elevated out of an abundance of caution. This is standard procedure.”

Earlier this month, the New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) warned of “extensive street closures and delays across Manhattan.”

At times, areas will be closed to both pedestrians and vehicles, including the Franklin D. Roosevelt East River Drive, Mamdani said.

A temporary flight restriction will also be in effect within a 2-nautical-mile radius of the UN until Saturday, according to Tisch.

The General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) began yesterday, with world leaders from dozens of countries delivering addresses and taking part in meetings.

Here’s a look back at some of the key events that took place yesterday:

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres delivered his opening remarks to kick off the day’s speeches, warning that the “fault lines in our world are widening.”

US President Donald Trump said that he has a “big decision” to make on Iran — casting it as a choice between striking a deal after the midterm elections or annihilating Iran.

Trump later said that members of his administration met with the Iranian delegation at UNGA for about three hours yesterday, in what he described vaguely as a “very good meeting.”

As Trump said during his address that Cuba’s communist government “will fall,” the Cuban delegation stood up and walked out of the room.

The US leader met with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the first time yesterday, with the pair bonding over their shared hope for Britain’s future.

Trump also met with acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez , as Washington maintains political pressure on her country to enact reforms.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he is ready to meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting with the US to end the war in Ukraine.

CNN’s Billy Stockwell, Maureen Chowdhury, Alejandra Jaramillo, Kit Maher, Michael Rios, Mitchell McCluskey, Maria Sole Campinoti, and Daria Tarasova-Markina contributed to this reporting.

Senior US and Iranian officials held talks in New York for the first time in more than three months yesterday as President Donald Trump outlined Iran’s options: reach an agreement or face “annihilation.”

As the war entered its seventh month, US special envoy Steve Witkoff held “lengthy talks” with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi through mediators, the highest-level diplomatic contact between the warring parties since a ceasefire agreed in June quickly unravelled.

It’s unclear what the parties discussed during several hours of talks, and no significant breakthrough was reported. In customary fashion, Iranian media said Araghchi reiterated Tehran’s general demands, including the unfreezing of Iranian assets, lifting of the US’ naval blockade on the Islamic Republic, and an end to wars on “all resistance fronts.”

Whether that includes Yemen remains uncertain. Iran-backed Houthi rebels there have made significant advances and disrupted Saudi oil exports since the last round of talks.

Witkoff said on X that the talks were indirect, with mediators shuttling between the parties.

King Abdullah of Jordan was seen crossing his fingers in videos posted on X when asked after the meeting if a deal with Iran was possible.

“There’s a consensus that we need a way forward. That’s the only consensus,” US ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, told reporters after the meeting, a video showed.

Diplomacy between Iran and the US had stalled in recent months as the region descended into further uncertainty over how the war will end. The Strait of Hormuz is still in turmoil as shadow fleet of tankers carry fuel through drone-threatened waters and the US and Iran exchange sporadic strikes.

At first glance, the order of countries speaking at the UN General Assembly seems a bit random. It isn’t alphabetical. It isn’t organized by region. And, though the US went second, it isn’t really organized by any metric of geopolitical power.

The system is more complicated than that. Ever since 1955, Brazil has opened the debate (except for 1983 and 1984) because “in the very early times, when no one wanted to speak first, Brazil always offered to speak first,” Desmond Parker, then the UN’s chief of protocol, told NPR in 2010.

The US then speaks second since it hosts the event. After that, a mixture of factors determines the order, including what representative a country sends, what date they applied to speak and keeping a geographic balance in the lineup.

“Everyone else follows in the order of the date at which the request was made. So, if we opened the speaker’s list as of the 10th of May, everyone who has applied to speak on the 11th of May will earn an early slot,” Parker said.

“The actual order is determined by precedence, meaning that heads of state speak first, followed by heads of government, followed by vice presidents, crown princes, ministers of foreign affairs and then other deputy ministers.”

This week, dozens of world leaders are gathering at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, where the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) will take place.

UNGA was established in 1945, the same year that the UN was founded, and is the “chief deliberative, policymaking and representative organ” of the organization, its website says.

The assembly is made up of all 193 United Nations members, who vote on important international issues and take part in high-level debates.

The UNGA also “makes recommendations to States on international issues within its competence,” including political, economic, humanitarian, social and legal matters, it says.

The theme for this year’s general debate at UNGA is “restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all,” according to the UN’s website.

Every year, an UNGA president is elected by the assembly’s members. The post rotates among the UN’s five regional groups: African States, Asia-Pacific States, Eastern European States, Latin American and Caribbean States and Western European and other States.

The president of this year’s UNGA session is Khalilur Rahman, the foreign minister of Bangladesh, whose program is designed around “six interlocking pillars.”

One of these “pillars” involves encouraging the peaceful resolution of conflicts, the protection of civilians, upholding international humanitarian law, and fighting against intolerance, hate speech, and disinformation.

Other “pillars” are focused on topics including sustainability, protecting human rights, digital governance and multilateralism.

During his speech to the UN General Assembly yesterday, US President Donald Trump spoke about many of the biggest geopolitical issues but didn’t really deliver any big surprises.

On Iran: Most notably, he weighed a “ big decision ” on Iran, threatening to either “annihilate” the country or strike a deal, likely after the US midterm elections in November.

He boasted that Tehran’s power in the Middle East has been broken by the war and denied the US is low on munitions, despite a recent report from the Pentagon’s official watchdog acknowledging the depletion of key US munition stockpiles amid the war with Iran.

On Cuba: Trump also threatened Cuba , saying its communist government “will fall,” prompting the country’s delegation to walk out the room. He said his administration is “seeking a fundamental change” in Cuba, before noting that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is leading negotiations with Havana.

On Greenland: He announced the US will “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence” in Greenland . The US has operated a military base on the Arctic territory since 1951.

On AI: Trump once again dismissed calls to slowdown the development of AI , saying he won’t “stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution.”

CNN’s Alayna Treene, Alejandra Jaramillo and Maureen Chowdhury contributed to this reporting.

After dozens of world leaders addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York yesterday, another 37 are set to speak today.

Here’s a look at who is scheduled this morning:

First to address UNGA today will be Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. Last year, he became the first Syrian leader to do so in almost 60 years, after toppling the Assad regime in December 2024.

Speaking fifth will be Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. His visit to the New York City comes as the US-Iran war is ongoing.

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky will be the 17th leader to speak this morning. At a press conference on the sidelines of the assembly yesterday, Zelensky said that he is ready to meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting with the US to end the war in his country

Leaders from another 18 countries are also set to speak this morning, including the heads of state from Latvia, Romania, Burundi, Paraguay, the Czech Republic, Argentina, Estonia and Timor Leste.

The leaders of Libya, Palau, Cyprus, the Dominican Republic, Botswana, Ecuador, Bulgaria, the Central African Republic, Panama and Ethiopia are also scheduled.

Will bring you the major lines from speeches as they happen.

The Trump administration will convene a high-level event on artificial intelligence on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly Wednesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter tell CNN, as the issue is expected to loom large over the global gathering.

The US event, to which multiple countries have been invited, comes as questions of AI and security have taken on new urgency amid dire warnings about the potential existential threat posed by artificial intelligence.

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has raged against the idea of government regulations, alleging concerns about the technology are a “hoax. ”

The US event is slated to take place the same day as a UN Security Council meeting on AI and security, to discuss the risks being seen by AI companies and executives. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is expected to brief that meeting, an OpenAI spokesperson told CNN.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, Undersecretary of State for Economic Growth, Energy, and the Environment Jacob Helberg, and Undersecretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah Rogers will host the US event.

The US is billing it as chance to talk about partnering with the US on AI, according to a source familiar with the event, and there is expected to be a discussion about the “policy, legal, and regulatory conditions that enable adoption at scale, including free expression considerations.”

CNN has reached out to the State Department for comment.

All eyes are on New York this week as world leaders gather for a high-level meeting of the UN General Assembly, the organization’s main policymaking body, where all its member states are represented.

Historically, the assembly has passed some landmark resolutions but its impact has lessened in recent years.

In 1948, member states adopted both the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Genocide Convention, providing the basis for modern international human rights law.

Later, in 1956, the assembly established the first ever UN peacekeeping force during the Suez Canal Crisis to supervise the withdrawal of French, British and Israeli troops from Egypt.

The assembly also approved the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) in 1968, which aimed to stop more countries developing nuclear weapons.

Almost every country joined except Israel, India and Pakistan, while North Korea withdrew from the treaty in 2003, displaying the UN’s limited ability to compel countries to stick to its resolutions. And in 1996, UNGA adopted the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, helping to almost completely curb the practice.

More recently, however, its resolutions have become less concrete in nature. The assembly endorsed the Responsibility to Protect doctrine in 2005 and established the Human Rights Council in 2006.

In 2015 it adopted the Sustainable Development Goals seeking to end poverty, turbocharge climate action and reduce inequality, but progress has been slow in some areas and non-existent in others.

Today at the UN General Assembly, we’re expecting a big speech from Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian, the day after US President Donald Trump threatened to “annihilate” the country as he weighed his “big decision” of whether to strike a deal with Tehran.

Shortly after Trump’s remarks, his special envoy Steve Witkoff said US and Iranian delegations engaged in “lengthy” indirect talks via mediators throughout the day on the sidelines of the summit.

They discussed reopening the Strait of Hormuz as well as Iran’s demands to lift the US naval blockade, release frozen assets and an end to the war on all “resistance fronts,” Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported. Trump added that there is another meeting “scheduled in the very near future,” without specifying any details.

Pezeshkian will be the fifth speaker in the morning session, before Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez will also speak later today.

With so many world leaders and top diplomats in one place for this meeting, diplomacy happens on and off the stage. Zelensky spoke with Trump yesterday in what he characterized as a “positive and productive meeting,” in which they discussed “a winter package of air defense for Ukraine.”

Rodríguez too met with Trump for the first time since the US ousted her predecessor Nicolás Maduro in January. She said they discussed “advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security.”

Elsewhere today, Prince Harry is appearing on a panel at the Clinton Global Initiatve – an event on the sidelines of the assembly – and the UN Security Council will meet this afternoon to discuss artificial intelligence.

CNN’s Kit Maher, Mitchell McCluskey, Eyad Kourdi and Daria Tarasova-Markina contributed reporting.

articles.title: Freedom should be on the agenda when Xi comes to Washington
articles.summary: As President Donald Trump prepares to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping, experts urge him to prioritize the release of political prisoners like Jimmy Lai and Joshua Wong to assert American leadership and defend democratic values.
articles.body:
Freedom has been prominent in our national debate and celebrations in this 250th anniversary year, reflecting its centrality to our country. As the White House prepares to host Chinese President Xi Jinping, freedom should once again be on the agenda.

As he did in his May meeting with Xi, President Trump should raise the cases of political prisoners held unfairly by the Chinese Communist Party.

Visible U.S. advocacy for the release of those unjustly imprisoned is not merely a humanitarian gesture; it’s an appeal for justice and a strategic imperative to reassert international norms and American global leadership. Members of the U.S. Congress should also raise these cases in their communication during Xi’s visit.

During the May Trump-Xi summit, the U.S. president highlighted several prominent cases, including Christian Pastor Ezra Jin who was arrested in October 2025 along with nearly 30 fellow clergy and workers. These arrests galvanized widespread condemnation and advocacy among American faith communities, human rights groups, Congress, and the White House. Jin was released and sent to the U.S. on July 3. Trump deserves credit for joining his voice with this large swell of advocacy for Jin.

As Trump meets with Xi this month, there are four important cases that deserve presidential engagement. Each person is sitting in prison for exercising freedoms that we hold dear in the U.S., including freedom of religion, speech and assembly.

Jimmy Lai , a British and Hong Kong citizen and businessman, has been imprisoned since 2020. He received a harsh sentence in late 2025 for peaceful protests, publishing pro-democracy articles and meeting with individuals from democratic nations.

Trump raised his case with Xi in 2025 and 2026. The State Department rightfully called his conviction an “enforcement of Beijing’s laws to silence those who seek to protect freedom of speech and other fundamental rights.”

At age 78, in failing health, and, importantly, innocent of any wrongdoing, Lai should be released immediately.

Joshua Wong , a 29-year-old Hong Kong opponent of Beijing’s crackdowns in the territory, has been imprisoned for peacefully protesting and collaborating with foreign democratic activists and governments, what is considered conspiracy to commit subversion under Hong Kong’s draconian security laws.

He has been in prison since November 2020 and was recently sentenced to an additional six years for a manufactured charge of foreign collusion. He deserves to be set free.

Dr. Gulshan Abbas , a retired physician, has been held unjustly by China for almost eight years. She was forcibly disappeared and sentenced to 20 years in prison by the Chinese government in retribution for the advocacy by her sister, prominent Uyghur activist Rushan Abbas, for their community in Xinjiang province. Abbas has been held in a reeducation camp without contact to her family. She deserves to be released immediately.

Fourteen of Jin’s colleagues were released in November and June, but the remaining eight have committed no crimes and are targeted for their Christian faith. Their names are Pastor Gao Yingjia, Pastor Wang Lin, Pastor Yin Huibin, Pastor Lin Shucheng, Pastor Liu Zhenbin, Pastor Wang Cong, Elder Wang Zhong, and Ms. Wu Qiuyu.

Getting on the agenda for the Trump-Xi visit is likely a competitive process, as is always the case for such strategic visits . But these political prisoner cases deserve to be raised repeatedly with the Chinese government. Defending freedom of religion and speech are both central to American values and core to the strategic competition we find ourselves in with China.

China is actively working to shift the global system to one in which rights are no longer protected but rather doled out at the whim of a dictator. And it is actively working to supplant American global leadership and reshape a new global order built not on democratic values but on their autocratic vision.

For those reasons, China is aligned with Russia, Iran and North Korea, which share a desire to shape a world where their tyranny will go unchecked. China’s continued purchase of Iranian oil and reported sharing of dual-use technology for military purposes will likely be on the Trump-Xi agenda. Silencing courageous individuals is also a shared tactic between Beijing, Moscow, Tehran and Pyongyang, and deserves to be part of the discussion when the two leaders meet.

Autocrats’ shared commitment to silencing opposition is a reflection of their fear of their own people, a weakness that the U.S. and other democracies can leverage. By supporting these opposition leaders, we not only support democratic allies but also undermine our most ardent adversaries in an area of significant vulnerability.

If Trump does not raise political prisoner cases, Xi will know that he can outwait the U.S. on issues of freedom. Rather than risking perceived retreat from the cases the president has raised in previous meetings with Xi, he should show that freedom remains central to America’s foreign policy agenda and leadership in the world.

These political prisoners are democratic allies in pushing back on the China-Russia-Iran-North Korea club of autocrats. It’s now our turn to be their champion for freedom.

Nicole Bibbins Sedaca is a democracy and foreign policy expert and fellow at the George W. Bush Institute.
