articles.title: Venezuela is crying out for free elections. The US can make it happen.
articles.summary: Through Operation Absolute Resolve, the United States succeeded in disarming the dictator; now it is time to dismantle the dictatorship.
articles.body:
The Jan. 3 capture of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro marked a turning point. Operation Absolute Resolve demonstrated that Trump’s revival of Monroe Doctrine was in effect, and that drug traffickers were not above the law or beyond the borders. This extraordinary mission, carried out more than eight months ago, leaves an outstanding obligation: holding free, fair and transparent elections.

The U.S. oil agreement with Venezuela that ensures 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves was a step in the right direction. It promotes investments and good paying jobs in Venezuela but also strengthens U.S. energy dominance and lower gas prices in the country. This strategic move ensures that bad actors like China, Russia and Iran will no longer profit from these invaluable resources.

After the successes of Operation Absolute Resolve and the historic oil deal, relations with Venezuela are at a crossroads. The U.S. must decide whether to strengthen a pragmatic business relationship with an illegitimate government, or to set a date for elections and support the resurgence of a prosperous, democratic nation.

Although the answer might seem simple, it is not always so. Authoritarian regimes often offer a false sense of temporary stability, whereas democracy is a complex and challenging process. Yet the latter is the right path for planting the foundations of lasting, deep-rooted prosperity.

In March 2016, President Barack Obama visited Cuba and chose to believe there was a difference between Raúl Castro and Fidel Castro — that the new dictator was someone with whom a pragmatic coexistence was possible. The famous Cuban thaw was a total disaster. That year alone, the Cuban dictatorship arrested 10,000 people and tightened its iron grip on power, all while receiving millions of U.S. dollars facilitated by the easing of restrictions under Obama’s pragmatic policies.

But the utopia of friendly relations with confirmed tyrants is nothing new. In the late 1990s, President Bill Clinton pursued a policy of more practical relations with Communist China. The prevailing belief was that greater trade openness would foster the growth of a middle class and drive a gradual shift toward democracy.

“The more we bring China into the world, the more the world will bring change and freedom to China,” Clinton said . The story ended badly; China remains a repressive dictatorship, but now with greater economic and military power.

There is a long history of pragmatic relations devoid of democracy or real change. They never had a happy ending. That is why elections in Venezuela are not merely an option, but the only path to ensuring that the outcome is not just a transaction, but a genuine transition.

Guyana , Venezuela’s small neighbor, is one of the fastest-growing economies in the world. According to the World Bank, real GDP growth in 2024 was 43.8 percent. It is estimated that this small nation will earn over $6 billion in oil revenue this year. It stands as an example of democracy and a reliable partner to the U.S.

According to the United Nations , Guyana’s recent general elections were more than just a civic exercise; they were an opportunity to strengthen public confidence in the democratic process. Indeed, prosperity and democracy are the right combination.

Delcy Rodriguez, a ruler never elected by the Venezuelan people, is not part of the solution; she is part of the problem.

Rodriguez knows that with each passing day, she must work to normalize her regime — not to relinquish power, but to hold on to it. To that end, her regime has handed over enriched uranium , released some political prisoners, minimally eased restrictions on the free press, and for the first time in 18 years, opened its doors to Human Rights Watch.

Venezuela’s interim government is willing to change as much as it needs to, so long as nothing actually changes.

Through Operation Absolute Resolve, the U.S. succeeded in disarming the dictator; now it is time to dismantle the dictatorship. The people of Venezuela want free elections. The U.S. has the power to make that happen, at the right time and in the right way.

It is time to finish the job. Let’s set the date.

Arturo McFields is an exiled journalist, former Nicaraguan ambassador to the Organization of American States, and a former member of the Norwegian Peace Corps. He is an alumnus of the National Defense University’s Security and Defense Seminar and the Harvard Leadership course.

articles.body: Ranchi: Southern and adjoining central districts of Jharkhand are likely to receive heavy to very heavy rain on Thursday as a deep depression over the Bay of Bengal moves inland, the Ranchi Meteorological Centre said on Wednesday.Very heavy rain is expected at isolated places in Simdega and West Singhbhum, while Ranchi, Khunti and Gumla may also receive intense showers. articles.title: ICC convicts former Central African Republic militia leader
articles.summary: Mahamat Said Abdel Kani oversaw brutal detention tactics, including torture, at Bangui facility, ICC judges rule.
articles.body:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has convicted a Central African Republic militia commander of crimes against humanity, including torture .

Judges in The Hague on Wednesday found Mahamat Said Abdel Kani guilty over his role of running a Seleka detention facility in Bangui, where supporters of then-President Francois Bozize were rounded up and tortured during the country’s 2013 civil war.

Said, 56, was acquitted of three war crimes charges as the judges ruled that the armed conflict had already ended when some of the alleged crimes happened.

A separate hearing will determine his sentence.

Judge Miatta Maria Samba said Said oversaw the torture at the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry, where detainees were whipped, waterboarded and bound using a method called “Arbatacher”, in which detainees’ hands, elbows and feet are tied together behind their backs.

Some prisoners were held in underground cells with no bathrooms or showers.

“The floor was covered in waste, and it smelled of faeces and urine,” Samba said.

She said a victim described how his life had been destroyed by the mistreatment.

Said, who denied the charges, appeared in court in jeans and a blue sweatshirt, looking unbothered as he shook his head when the verdict was read.

He was a senior figure in the Seleka coalition, which ousted Bozize in 2013, plunging the country into a conflict that killed thousands of people.

Bozize’s response, arming the “anti-Balaka” militia, fuelled more bloodshed before French troops helped secure the country in 2014 under a United Nations mandate.

The ICC has investigated violence in the Central African Republic since 2014 and has already convicted two anti-Balaka leaders, including former Sports Minister Patrice-Edouard Ngaissona, who was sentenced to 12 years, and former MP Alfred Yekatom who was sentenced to 15 years.

Said is the first Seleka member to be convicted.

The country has experienced relative stability since a 2019 peace agreement.

articles.title: RAF plane crash on Anglesey as two pilots eject
articles.summary: North Wales Police said the pilots of the RAF T2 Hawk aircraft are being treated for minor injuries.
articles.body:
Two pilots ejected and parachuted out of their plane before a crash involving an RAF training aircraft.

North Wales Police said the pilots of the RAF T2 Hawk aircraft were being treated for minor injuries following the incident in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey.

The force said helicopters from the Coastguard and the Wales Air Ambulance were at the scene close to RAF Valley on the island.

"Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries," it said.

"Please avoid the area until further notice."

The Ministry of Defence has been asked to comment.

The Royal Air Force said: "An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley.

"An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time."

articles.title: Capt. Sully Sullenberger speaks out about Alzheimer’s diagnosis: ‘I’ve done harder things than this before’
articles.summary: For the first time since announcing his Alzheimer’s diagnosis over the summer, Capt. Sully Sullenberger discusses the impact on his life.
articles.body: For the first time since announcing his Alzheimer’s diagnosis over the summer, Capt. Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger has discussed his experience with the disease and what lies ahead. “I’ve done harder things than this before,” Sullenberger, the retired pilot who successfully landed a commercial airliner filled with passengers on the Hudson River in 2009, told “Good Morning America” on Wednesday. Sullenberger, 75, and his wife, Lorrie Sullenberger, spoke to host Robin Roberts about the diagnosis, which he revealed in a post on his website in July. “I recently found out I have been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s Disease. It is early stage,” Sullenberger wrote in the July 14 post. “For now, this means a name may not come easily to me, I forget a story I have recently told, or I don’t sleep as well, but I am in the beginning of this long journey.” Sullenberger became a household name when he successfully landed a commercial airplane in the Hudson River, saving everyone on board, after a bird strike caused both engines to fail shortly after takeoff. The act has since been known as “The Miracle on the Hudson.” Clint Eastwood dramatized Sullenberger’s heroic exploits in the 2016 film “Sully,” starring Tom Hanks in the titular role. Roberts on Wednesday asked Sullenberger to compare his diagnosis to that heroic moment. “We had to devise a plan, execute that plan flawlessly for the first time — never having done it before — and save every life in 208 seconds,” Sullenberger recalled. He added, “had even one person not survived, I would have considered it a tragic failure.” “So I think we’re we’re doing the same thing here,” he continued of his diagnosis. “We’re focusing clearly on the highest priority items first, and we are ignoring everything we don’t have time to do.” Sullenberger is receiving monthly treatments for the disease, which aims to slow the condition. Both he and his wife said initially, they wanted to keep his diagnosis private, but later decided to speak out with the hope that they could help others. “This is a disease, not a character flaw,” Lorrie Sullenberger said. “I think we need to talk about it more openly, and maybe other people can do the same.” Sullenberger added that at first, he questioned: “Why me?” But, “we’re not by any means alone,” he reflected. “We’re part of this community who are trying to make the best of a bad situation.” Sullenberger said the first signs of the disease were forgetting things that he normally wouldn’t, like people’s names — even those he has known for a long time — and events. The symptoms were easy to dismiss in the beginning, his wife said, because they were so minor. She noted that what a lot of people see in the news are cases of late-stage Alzheimer’s disease. “If you have doubts, get tested because the sooner you act, the more options there are, the better the outcome is likely to be,” Sullenberger said. One of the couple’s daughters, Kelly Sullenberger, told Roberts that since her dad’s diagnosis, her priority has been spending more time with their family. “Our family likes to be prepared and have plans in place. It runs in our blood, and it’s something that you can’t really plan for,” she said. Sullenberger, who is set to be inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame this month, told Roberts that his greatest concern is “that this is my last flight.” “But if this has to be my last flight,” he said, “I’m going to go out using full afterburner.”
